 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

        COME NOW Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”), LCRA Transmission

Services Corporation (“LCRA TSC”), AEP Texas, Inc., and the City of San Antonio, acting

through the City Public Service Board (“CPS Energy”) (collectively, “Joint TSPs”),

and respectfully submit this response to the Brief of Certain Texas Legislators as Amici Curiae in

Support of American Stewards of Liberty, Inc.’s (“ASL’s”) Motion to Defer Determination of

Need (“Motion to Defer”),1 as filed in each of the above-referenced dockets, respectfully showing

as follows:

                                         I.    INTRODUCTION

        On June 5, 2026, ASL filed its Motion to Defer, which asked the Commission to defer a

determination on the need for the 765 kV import paths approved as part of the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan until the completion of Docket No. 59475.2 On June 15, 2026, certain Texas

Legislators (“Signatories”) filed an amicus brief in support of ASL’s Motion to Defer.3 The

Motion to Defer and Amicus Brief are inconsistent with the governing laws and regulations on

more than one account.

        First, ASL’s Motion to Defer relies on an outdated Commission rule, as opposed to Public

Utility Regulatory Act4 (“PURA”) § 37.057, which governs the timeline for approval of

applications for new transmission facilities. Second, ASL and the Signatories seek to delay this

 proceeding to promote alternative policies that are inconsistent with existing market structure in

the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) and the Commission’s authority under

PURA. The 88th Texas Legislature duly enacted House Bill (“H.B.”) 5066,5 which directed the

Commission and ERCOT, as the entities responsible for transmission access, reliability, and

planning,6 to develop and implement a plan to provide reliable transmission service in the Permian

Basin region.

        While the Motion to Defer requests a delay of all 765 kV proceedings until the completion

of Docket No. 59475, the Signatories advocate for a complete pause of the 765 kV import paths

until ERCOT fully evaluates purported non-transmission alternatives, such as increasing local

generation capacity.7 But neither ERCOT nor the Commission has authority over the siting,

timing, or construction of new generation under PURA chapter 39. Under the market design that

exists today, questions of whether, where, and when to build new generation facilities are

“determined by customer choices and the normal forces of competition.”8 Furthermore, H.B. 5066

does not contemplate the development of new generation, and it does not authorize the

Commission to order new generation to be built at a specific time and place, as would be required

to implement any plan dependent on increasing generation capacity. While the Signatories do not

directly assert that the Commission has such authority, they suggest that hypothetical market

reforms or incentives could be a viable substitute. To be clear, such a market structure does not

presently exist and may never be implemented, so it cannot form the basis for the critical reliability

needs of the Permian Basin Region and the greater ERCOT electric grid today and in the

foreseeable future.

        In response to the legislative mandate of H.B. 5066, ERCOT and the Commission spent

almost two years comprehensively studying and evaluating the reliability needs of the Permian

Basin and the statewide transmission system and deliberating on all possible viable alternatives.

This process led ERCOT to recommend, and the Commission to approve, three 765 kV import

paths as the best solution based on the directive of the Legislature. The Signatories now ask the

Commission to set aside the express requirements of H.B. 5066. Doing so would have serious

ramifications for the reliability of the Permian Basin and the broader ERCOT system.

       Finally, ASL and the Signatories address their pleadings to the Commission. But these

dockets were referred to SOAH, and all but one remain with SOAH. The SOAH Administrative

Law Judges (“ALJs”) are the presiding officers over these proceedings and will remain as such

until they issue proposals for decision (“PFDs”) and remand the respective matters to the

Commission.     The SOAH ALJs are managing the existing dockets pursuant to orders of the

Commission and are without authority from the Commission to grant the relief requested by ASL

and the Signatories. For the reasons established herein, ASL’s Motion to Defer must be denied.

                                      II.    ARGUMENT

       A. The Record Evidence Establishes the Need for the 765 kV Import Paths

       ASL and the Signatories argue that it would be “premature” to issue a decision on the need

for any import path now because evidence may still come to light that calls their necessity into

question. ASL has offered no such evidence. The Signatories explain that they do not seek

intervention, party status, or expansion of the issues in this proceeding; but they offer a paper from

the Texas Public Policy Foundation (“TPPF”), which they say raises questions about the need for

the Permian Basin import paths.9 As a threshold matter, the Brief of Certain Legislators and the



9
       Brief of Certain Legislators at 3-4, Att. A.
JOINT TSPS’ RESPONSE TO BRIEF OF CERTAIN TEXAS LEGISLATORS

                                             Page 6 of 17
 TPPF paper attached is not evidence in the record and should be treated as public comment. No

party had an opportunity to propound discovery regarding the TPPF paper, address it in rebuttal

testimony, or cross-examine any witness on it. It therefore does not satisfy the requirements for

admission into evidence under the Administrative Procedure Act or the Commission’s procedural

rules. The ALJs and ultimately the Commission must decide each case based on the evidence

admitted into the record in that proceeding.10 Docket No. 59475 is the only import path proceeding

where the record has not yet closed. Even if the TPPF paper were admitted in evidence in that

docket, it could not be considered as part of the decision-making process in Docket Nos. 59029,

59315, or 59336, and Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475 are already consolidated on the issue of need,

rendering ASL’s request for a deferral moot. It would be contrary to the Commission’s procedural

rules and the Texas Administrative Procedure Act for the ALJs and the Commission to consider

information that has not been established through the evidentiary record in Docket Nos. 59029,

59182, 59315, or 59336.11

        Moreover, the record in each pending 765 kV docket contains substantial evidence that the

765 kV import paths are critically needed. ERCOT conducted months of extensive and well-

documented analysis to identify the transmission improvements needed to reliably serve the

Permian Basin.       A major component of this analysis was the substantive, public-facing

involvement of Commission Staff, TSPs, existing and developing generation resources, and other

stakeholders, through requests for public comments, formal requests for information, public

workshops, and multiple Regional Planning Group meetings.12

         ERCOT performed reliability assessments under the applicable NERC reliability

standards, which showed post-contingency thermal overloads and voltage violations under N-0

(system intact) conditions that could not be solved without new transmission import paths.13 Even

after publishing the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, ERCOT continued to perform extensive

reliability, economic, and power-loss studies in conjunction with the 2024 Regional Transmission

Plan (“RTP”) to determine whether 765 kV import paths were needed. In January 2024, ERCOT

published its 345-kV Plan and Texas 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (“STEP”)

Comparison, which demonstrates that a 765 kV alternative significantly outperforms a lower-

voltage solution with regard to statewide costs and benefits.14 Specifically, ERCOT identified the

following benefits of the 765 kV STEP compared with a 345 kV alternative:

            •   Reduction of consumer congestion costs by $229 million annually;
            •   Reduction of system production costs by $28 million annually;
            •   Reduction of energy losses by 560 GWh annually, which is equivalent to a 128 MW
                thermal unit operating at a 50% capacity factor,
            •   Increase of up to 3,000 MW in power transfer capability; and
            •   Increase in system West Texas stability limit by 13%.15
        Based on the overwhelming benefits at a comparable cost to the 345 kV alternative,

ERCOT “strongly recommend[ed]” the 765 kV STEP.16 ERCOT’s recommendation is entitled to

great evidentiary weight from the Commission.17

        B. The Purpose of the Requested Delay is Inconsistent with PURA

       The Signatories suggest that a delay will allow ERCOT to consider alternatives such as

adding dispatchable generation capacity near customer loads in the Permian Basin.18 This

suggestion is inconsistent with the market design established in PURA chapter 39. The Signatories

acknowledge this fact, stating they “do not suggest that the Commission can command private

generation investment outside the governing market structure[;]” yet they argue that the

Commission should “test” the need for the import paths against other “reasonable alternatives

including market reforms and incentives,” which are equally outside the Commission’s authority

to implement.19

       While the Commission retains limited authority over electricity generation in areas such as

weatherization, provision of ancillary services, and monitoring for market power abuses, this

authority has not, and cannot, compel the construction of new generation at the scale or on the

timeline needed to meet the needs of the Permian Basin. That authority is simply not a tool the

Legislature has given the Commission. For example, under PURA chapter 39, even if the

Commission finds an abuse of market power associated with competitive generation or finds that

the State’s electric markets require additional electricity, its primary tool to address that situation

is to order the construction of additional transmission or distribution facilities.20

       A fundamental objective of the current ERCOT market structure is to enable private entities

to decide when and where to build new generation based on customer choice, market forces, and

competition.21 Even if ERCOT had created a generation-based plan to “test” the need for the

import paths, neither ERCOT nor the Commission could implement such a plan—or glean any

reforms or incentives and the economic motivations of power generation companies are entirely

beyond its control. Therefore, studying such a plan would not yield actionable results.

        C. H.B. 5066 Requires a Transmission Reliability Plan

        The Signatories state that “the Legislature never suggested that extensive new transmission

lines were the answer to the Permian Basin’s electricity needs.” They also assert that, unlike the

Competitive Renewable Energy Zone transmission buildout, the Permian Basin Reliability Plan

“was approved without comparable legislative authorization.” These statements are inconsistent

with H.B. 5066, which was titled “An Act Relating to Electricity Service in Areas of This State

with a Need for Transmission Projects.”22 The Legislature’s bill analysis described H.B. 5066 as

“intended to spur a bolder, more proactive approach that better syncs transmission planning and

construction process with the dynamic needs of Texas customers.”23                     H.B. 5066 expressly

designates the Permian Basin as a region “in which transmission capacity is insufficient”24 and

required ERCOT to develop a plan that would “(1) address extending transmission service to areas

where mineral resources have been found; (2) address increasing available capacity to meet

forecasted load; and (3) provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas

without access to transmission service.” H.B. 5066 further requires the Commission to “develop

a plan to implement [the Permian Basin Reliability Plan] to ensure timely development and

approval of necessary transmission service improvements.”25 Respectfully, the Signatories’ post

hoc interpretation of H.B. 5066 is unable to overcome the plain language of the statute, which was

duly enacted by the Texas Legislature with a combined vote of 170-3.

         While H.B. 5066 makes no mention of generation alternatives, it is significant that the 88th

Texas Legislature enacted a different piece of legislation alongside H.B. 5066 that was tailored to

the competitive market for generation. Senate Bill (“S.B.”) 2627 established the Texas Energy

Fund (“TEF”) to spur the development of new dispatchable generation through a market-based

incentive program.26 As of April 2026, almost three years after S.B. 2627 took effect, ERCOT

counted only 2.5 GW of planned TEF generation in Far West Texas, all of which are still in the

due diligence phase.27 By comparison, ERCOT modeled approximately 17 GW of planned

generation capacity in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan,28 and almost 60 GW (i.e., all planned

resources in ERCOT’s interconnection queue) in the 2024 RTP.29 Both the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan and the 2024 RTP affirmed the need for the 765 kV import paths, with ERCOT

declaring in the 2024 RTP that all three 765 kV import paths are “critical components” of its Core

Plan needed by 2030.30

        D. The Permian Basin Needs More Transmission Capacity Now

        ERCOT’s recent announcement of two new Generic Transmission Constraints (“GTCs”)

on the West Texas transmission system underscores the urgent need for the 765 kV import paths.31

In contrast to the West Texas Export Interface, which restricts power flows out of the Permian

Basin, the North to Far West (“N-FW”) and South to Far West (“S-FW”) Import GTCs restrict

power flows into the Permian Basin.32 ERCOT actively monitors these GTCs as Interconnection

 Reliability Operating Limits (“IROLs”) and carefully manages power flows over each GTC to

avoid exceeding those limits, which could cause cascading thermal overloads across Far West

Texas.33 Even at today’s load levels, ERCOT has stated that emergency actions, including pre-

contingency firm load shed, may be necessary to prevent widespread, uncontrolled power

outages.34 This risk is greatest during low-wind, no-solar conditions, when the Permian Basin

relies heavily on imports over the 345 kV transmission network to meet demand.35 These

conditions occur regularly in Far West Texas. When they do, the ERCOT’s ability to avoid firm

load shed is currently dependent on the voluntary demand response of cryptocurrency customers

and the uninterrupted availability of all dispatchable units and all transmission import paths serving

the region.36 If just one of those generators experienced a maintenance outage or one of the

existing import paths went down due to an unplanned outage electric demand could exceed the

available supply.37

        In addition to signaling the need for new transmission capacity, the West Texas GTCs also

create significant impediments to the free-market’s development of new dispatchable generation

capacity in the Permian Basin. The congestion on the West Texas transmission system often

requires generation curtailment that prevents Permian Basin generation from being sold in other

parts of the State.38 This forces Permian Basin dispatchable generators to directly compete in a

limited region of ERCOT with the abundant, low-cost wind and solar resources in that area.

        E. H.B. 5066 Repeatedly Emphasized that Time is of the Essence

        The Legislature repeatedly emphasized that time is of the essence for the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan, building several aggressive deadlines into H.B. 5066. First, the Legislature

required the Commission to order ERCOT to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin no

later than January 30, 2024.42 Next, H.B. 5066 required the Commission to “develop a plan to

implement [the Permian Basin Reliability Plan] to ensure timely development and approval of

necessary transmission service improvements.”43 Then, H.B. 5066 required the Commission to

consider whether “electrical load cannot be interconnected in a timely manner” when evaluating

applications for new transmission facilities.44 Finally, H.B. 5066 shortened the statutory timeline

for new transmission line CCNs from one year to 180 days.45 These provisions demonstrate the

 Legislature’s expectation that the Commission will act promptly and decisively to approve

necessary transmission upgrades.

       The Commission cannot defer a decision on the import path CCN applications without

exceeding the 180-day deadline, which is codified at PURA § 37.057. Further, even a delay of a

few weeks or months in the projects being approved would increase construction costs and—given

ERCOT’s seasonal outage moratoriums and the difficulty of obtaining outages in West Texas even

during the construction season (another problem that can only be resolved with additional

transmission capacity)—may cause much longer downstream delays that prevent the import paths

from being placed in service when they are needed.

       ASL and the Signatories incorrectly assert that the 180-day deadline for decision is eligible

for a good-cause extension, citing 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(D).46 That rule

predates the 180-day deadline in PURA § 37.057 and does not supersede the statutory

requirement.47 PURA § 37.057 does not provide for good-cause extensions, and there is no other

provision in PURA that allows the Commission to grant itself a good-cause extension to a duly

enacted statutory requirement.

       F. The Need for the 765 kV Import Paths Was Thoroughly Evaluated

       The Motion to Defer suggests that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan should be reevaluated

to ensure a “complete examination of the issues.” But ERCOT and the Commission thoroughly

examined the issues, including the full range of alternatives that are within their authority to

implement, for almost two years after H.B. 5066 took effect. In the Permian Basin Reliability

Plan, ERCOT evaluated import path options at three voltage classes to offer the Commission a full

range of alternatives. In October 2024, the Commission approved the Permian Basin Reliability

 Plan but deferred a decision on the voltage class until ERCOT could complete a more fulsome,

statewide study of the costs and benefits of the 765 kV and 345 kV alternatives.

       ERCOT published the 2024 RTP in December 2024, followed by the 345-kV Plan and

Texas 765-kV STEP Comparison in January 2025, which showed that the 765 kV STEP was the

superior alternative. Even then, the Commission evaluated ERCOT’s study results, took additional

public comments, and discussed the issue at multiple open meetings before finally approving the

765 kV alternative in April 2025. In other words, the deferral requested by ASL and the

Signatories has already happened. The 765 kV import paths are needed as soon as they can be

 Legislature's expectation that the Commission will act promptly and decisively to approve

       The Commission cannot defer a decision on the import path CCN applications without

exceeding the 180-day deadline, which is codified at PURA § 37.057. Further, even a delay of a

few weeks or months in the proj ects being approved would increase construction costs and-given

ERCOT's seasonal outage moratoriums and the difficulty of obtaining outages in West Texas even

during the construction season (another problem that can only be resolved with additional

transmission capacity)-may cause much longer downstream delays that prevent the import paths

from being placed in service when they are needed.

       ASL and the Signatories incorrectly assert that the 180-day deadline for decision is eligible

for a good-cause extension, citing 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(D).46 That rule

predates the 180-day deadline in PURA § 37.057 and does not supersede the statutory

requirement.47 PURA § 37.057 does not provide for good-cause extensions, and there is no other

provision in PURA that allows the Commission to grant itself a good-cause extension to a duly

enacted statutory requirement.

       F. The Need for the 765 kV Import Paths Was Thoroughly Evaluated

       The Motion to Defer suggests that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan should be reevaluated

to ensure a "complete examination of the issues." But ERCOT and the Commission thoroughly

examined the issues, including the full range of alternatives that are within their authority to

implement, for almost two years after H.B. 5066 took effect. In the Permian Basin Reliability

Plan, ERCOT evaluated import path options at three voltage classes to offer the Commission a full

range of alternatives. In October 2024, the Commission approved the Permian Basin Reliability

statewide study of the costs and benefits of the 765 kV and 345 kV alternatives.

       ERCOT published the 2024 RTP in December 2024, followed by the 345-kV Plan and

Texas 765-kV STEP Comparison in January 2025, which showed that the 765 kV STEP was the

superior alternative. Even then, the Commission evaluated ERCOT's study results, took additional

public comments, and discussed the issue at multiple open meetings before finally approving the

765 kV alternative in April 2025.     In other words, the deferral requested by ASL and the

Signatories has already happened. The 765 kV import paths are needed as soon as they can be

constructed. The Joint TSPs do not dispute that the Permian Basin would benefit from more

dispatchable generation capacity, but ERCOT' s transmission planning process is not the right

place to explore that option, and the Commission is not currently empowered to order that capacity

into existence.   Delay will not address the Permian Basin' s pressing needs but will instead

exacerbate those needs. There is no basis for granting ASL's Motion to Defer.
